fields.name: The Feudal World
fields.note: Castles, guilds, gutters and archaic speech — the register of historical fiction and fantasy.

fields.name: Faith & Philosophy
fields.note: How thinkers argue about scripture: literal or symbolic, human-shaped or beyond shape entirely.

fields.name: Power & Conflict
fields.note: What rulers do, what subjects endure, and what happens when either pushes too far.

fields.name: Rhetoric & Deception
fields.note: The vocabulary of political argument — most of these appear in news analysis and opinion writing.

fields.name: Character & Temperament
fields.note: Words that judge a person. Nearly all carry approval or contempt, so they are rarely neutral.

fields.name: Mind & Abstraction
fields.note: Formal, essay-register words. These lift academic and professional writing more than any other group here.

fields.name: Body, Vice & Survival
fields.note: The physical and the disreputable. A few are blunt — the notes tell you when to be careful.

fields.name: Hardship & Social Order
fields.note: Poverty, policing, and the language of who holds power over whom. This is the register of journalism and social science — and it is the field your list has grown into most.

words.d: A sworn oath of loyalty, especially from a vassal to a lord.
words.e: The knight knelt and pledged *fealty* to the new king.
words.a: وَلاء مُقسَم عليه — عهد التابع لسيّده

words.d: To formally promise someone in marriage.
words.e: The duke *betrothed* his daughter to the prince when she was still a child.

words.d: A fortified stronghold or keep. (In modern use it can also mean a clamp.)
words.e: The soldiers retreated to the *holdfast* on the hill and prepared to defend it.

words.d: To appoint someone as a priest — or, more broadly, to decree something by authority.
words.e: The king *ordained* that no merchant could trade without a royal permit.

words.d: Common people, peasants. Heavily used in fantasy writing.
words.e: The war meant nothing to the *smallfolk* — they suffered whoever won.

words.d: People who turn animal hides into leather. Their workshops were notoriously foul-smelling.
words.e: The *tanners'* district reeked so badly that no noble would ride through it.

words.d: Communal pit toilets, especially in camps and barracks.
words.e: The soldiers dug *latrines* at the edge of the camp before nightfall.

words.d: An inn where people drink, eat and sometimes sleep.
words.e: They found a warm *tavern* near the gate and ordered ale and bread.
words.a: حانة، نُزُل يُقدَّم فيه الشراب والمبيت

words.d: Charity — money or food given to the poor. Always plural; never 'an alm'.
words.e: The monks distributed *alms* to beggars outside the abbey every morning.

words.d: Treasure chests — and by extension, a government's or company's financial reserves.
words.e: The war emptied the kingdom's *coffers*, and the crown had to raise taxes.
words.a: صناديق المال — خزينة الدولة أو المؤسسة

words.d: A thick hot cereal made by boiling grain, usually oats, in water or milk.
words.e: The prisoners received nothing but thin *porridge* and stale bread.

words.d: An old term for a pharmacist — someone who prepared and sold medicines.
words.e: She visited the *apothecary* for a tincture to ease her headaches.

words.d: A woman living with a man in a marriage-like relationship but without a wife's legal standing.
words.e: The emperor's *concubine* wielded more influence at court than the empress herself.

words.d: A castrated man, historically employed as a palace guard or court official.
words.e: The *eunuch* served as the queen's most trusted advisor for thirty years.
words.a: خَصيّ — رجل مخصيّ كان يخدم في القصور

words.d: A woman who sews clothes for a living.
words.e: The *seamstress* worked by candlelight to finish the gown before the feast.

words.d: Castrated — normally said of horses.
words.e: They *gelded* the stallion to make him calmer for riding.
words.n: Applied to a man it is a severe insult, so keep it to animals.

words.d: A green gemstone — but in older writing, a worn-out horse or a disreputable woman.
words.e: The merchant tried to sell me that old *jade* of a horse for twice its worth.

words.d: A machine for weaving cloth. As a verb: to appear large and threatening.
words.e: Dark clouds *loomed* over the mountains, promising a violent storm.
words.a: نَوْل النسيج؛ وكفعل: يلوح مُهدِّدًا في الأفق

words.d: To fund something permanently with a gift of money or property.
words.e: The wealthy merchant *endowed* the building that would become the town's first library.
words.a: يُوقِف مالًا أو عقارًا لدعم مؤسسة

words.d: The 16th–18th-century theory that national wealth comes from maximising exports, hoarding gold and controlling colonial trade.
words.e: Under *mercantilism*, the colonies existed solely to enrich the mother country.
words.a: المذهب التجاري — نظرية ثروة الأمم بالتصدير وتكديس الذهب

words.d: An archaic word for 'perhaps'.
words.e: *Mayhaps* the king will grant us an audience, if we arrive before noon.
words.n: Nobody says this in modern speech. Use it only in historical or fantasy writing.

words.d: To linger, or to stay longer than intended.
words.e: Do not *tarry* — the enemy draws closer with every hour.

words.d: A monarch's spouse. As a verb, to associate with someone — usually disapprovingly.
words.e: You should not *consort* with known criminals.
words.a: قرين المَلِك أو المَلِكة؛ وكفعل: يُخالِط (بمعنى سلبي)

words.d: A place of refuge and safety; also the holiest part of a temple or church.
words.e: The fugitive sought *sanctuary* in the cathedral, where the guards could not follow.

words.d: A benefit or blessing; also a favour granted by someone powerful.
words.e: The general's victory was a *boon* to the whole kingdom.

words.d: Public respect or tribute. Originally the ceremony in which a vassal knelt and acknowledged his lord.
words.e: The film pays *homage* to the westerns its director grew up watching.
words.a: تكريم وإجلال؛ وأصلًا: مراسم بيعة التابع لسيّده

words.d: A permanent fund of money or property given to support an institution. Also, a natural gift a person is born with.
words.e: The university lives off the interest from its *endowment* rather than spending the capital.
words.a: وَقْف — مال دائم يُنفَق ريعُه على مؤسسة
words.n: The noun of 'endow' (entry above): you endow a college, and the money you gave becomes its endowment.

words.d: Reading a text in its exact, word-for-word sense, refusing symbolic readings.
words.e: His *literalism* led him to reject any figurative reading of the scriptures.

words.d: The attempt to understand God through reason and argument rather than faith alone.
words.e: *Rational theology* asks whether the existence of God can be proven by argument.

words.d: Attributing human form, emotions or body parts to God, animals or objects.
words.e: Describing God as having hands or feeling anger is a form of *anthropomorphism*.
words.a: التجسيم — نسبة صفات البشر وأعضائهم إلى الله

words.d: Working out what to do with passages that describe God in human terms.
words.e: Scholars spent centuries *interpreting anthropomorphic* verses — did God literally sit on a throne?

words.d: Reading a text as a symbolic story carrying a deeper hidden meaning.
words.e: An *allegorical understanding* of the flood sees it as spiritual renewal, not literal water.

words.d: Existence beyond ordinary experience and the physical world.
words.e: Mystics seek *transcendence* — an experience that lifts them above everyday reality.

words.d: The doctrine that God is wholly beyond the world and beyond human comprehension.
words.e: *Divine transcendence* means God cannot be fully grasped by the human mind.
words.a: تَنزيه الذات الإلهية — كون الله فوق الإدراك البشري

words.d: Treating a description as figurative rather than literal.
words.e: Rather than believing God has a literal hand, most theologians are *metaphorically interpreting* such passages.

words.d: Belief in, or worship of, many gods.
words.e: Ancient Greece practised *polytheism*, with gods for war, love and the sea.

words.d: Treating something sacred with violent disrespect.
words.e: The vandalism of the temple was condemned as an act of *desecration*.

words.d: Literally, to whip oneself as penance. Usually figurative: to punish yourself with excessive guilt.
words.e: There's no point *self-flagellating* over a mistake you can't undo.
words.a: يجلد ذاته — حرفيًّا كفارةً، ومجازًا: يُفرِط في لوم نفسه

words.d: Fragrant smoke burned in worship. As a verb (stress the second syllable): to enrage.
words.e: His arrogance *incensed* everyone in the room.
words.a: بَخُور؛ وكفعل (بنبرة أخرى): يُثير الغضب الشديد
words.n: Two different stresses: IN-cense the smoke, in-CENSE the anger.

words.d: Harsh official investigations into belief — historically, church tribunals prosecuting heresy.
words.e: The *inquisitions* terrorised the countryside — anyone could be accused.
words.a: محاكم التفتيش؛ تحقيقات قمعية في المعتقد

words.d: A sign believed to predict the future, usually something bad.
words.e: The villagers took the dead ravens as an *omen* of war.
words.a: فَأْل أو نَذير — علامة تُنذر بالمستقبل

words.d: Moderation and self-restraint, especially about alcohol.
words.e: The monk lived a life of *temperance* — no excess of any kind.
words.a: الاعتدال وضبط النفس، خاصة عن الخمر

words.d: Established by higher authority, as if by fate or divine will.
words.e: He believed the outcome had been *ordained* long before either army marched.
words.a: مُقدَّر، مقضيّ به من سلطة أعلى

words.d: Inciting rebellion against the authority of a state or ruler.
words.e: The pamphlets bore *seditious* markings and were burned by the city guard.

words.d: Extremely serious, urgent or dreadful.
words.e: The city faced *dire* consequences if the dam was not repaired before the rains.

words.d: Sudden impulsive desires or changes of mind.
words.e: The tyrant ruled by his *whims* — no one could predict what he'd command next.

words.d: Abandoning a duty, a post, or military service.
words.e: *Desertion* during wartime was punishable by death.
words.a: الفرار من الخدمة أو التخلّي عن الواجب

words.d: To endure something difficult and survive it. Past participle: ridden out.
words.e: The village had *ridden out* worse storms than this one.
words.a: يصمد في وجه شدّة حتى تمرّ

words.d: Blocked or frustrated — prevented from succeeding.
words.e: Her plans were *thwarted* by an unexpected betrayal within her own council.

words.d: To crush underfoot; figuratively, to treat something with contempt.
words.e: The cavalry *trampled* everything in its path as it charged through the village.

words.d: To strike back; to return an attack or injury.
words.e: If we *retaliate* now, it will only escalate the conflict further.

words.d: A violation of a law, a moral code, or a boundary.
words.e: He was exiled for his *transgressions* against the crown.

words.d: Noisy confusion, disorder and upheaval.
words.e: The announcement sent the crowd into *tumult* — shouting and shoving broke out at once.

words.d: To agree to a demand, usually reluctantly. Also, to take up high office.
words.e: Under pressure, the council finally *acceded* to the rebels' demands.
words.a: يَذعن ويوافق (على مضض)؛ أو يتولّى منصبًا

words.d: Unintended negative consequences of a political or covert action.
words.e: The sanctions produced serious *blowback* — public opinion turned against the government.
words.a: ارتداد عكسي — عواقب غير مقصودة لفعل سياسي

words.d: A trace of contamination, corruption or disgrace.
words.e: The scandal left a *taint* on his reputation that never fully faded.

words.d: Equipment for a purpose — or a large organisational machine, as in 'the state apparatus'.
words.e: The entire state *apparatus* was mobilised to respond to the crisis.
words.a: جهاز — معدّات؛ أو الجهاز التنظيمي للدولة

words.d: Rejected with contempt or disdain.
words.e: She *spurned* his proposal and left the room without another word.

words.d: A small pet dog — figuratively, someone who obeys a powerful person without question.
words.e: The minister was the president's *lapdog*; he never challenged a single decision.
words.a: كلب حِجْر — تابع ذليل ينفّذ دون اعتراض

words.d: Disorderly and difficult to control.
words.e: The *unruly* crowd pushed past the barricades and flooded into the square.

words.d: Imprisonment, or restriction to a limited space.
words.e: The prisoner spent six months in solitary *confinement*.

words.d: Weakening or suffering through a long, hopeless wait.
words.e: The prisoners of war were *languishing* in military detention, forgotten by the outside world.
words.a: يَذوي ويُعاني في انتظار طويل بلا أمل
words.n: Note the spelling: languish → languishing, not 'languishion'.

words.d: A specific condition attached to an agreement — the thing you insist on before you say yes.
words.e: She accepted the job with one *stipulation*: she would never work weekends.

words.d: To violently remove unwanted people from a party, army or country. Also, more mildly, to cleanse something of impurities.
words.e: The new leader *purged* the party of everyone who had opposed his rise.

words.d: Language deliberately designed to provoke anger or violence.
words.e: The politician's *incendiary rhetoric* stirred up hatred against immigrants.

words.d: Bold and shameless — done openly with no attempt to hide it.
words.e: His *brazen* bigotry shocked even those who had tolerated his earlier remarks.

words.d: Stubborn, hostile intolerance toward people of another group.
words.e: Her *bigotry* showed in every remark she made about the new neighbours.

words.d: Outrageously obvious — impossible to miss and impossible to excuse.
words.e: The report was full of *flagrant* lies that anyone could disprove in a single search.

words.d: To publicly adopt and promote a belief or cause.
words.e: The leader *espoused* genocidal comments that drew international condemnation.

words.d: Language that promotes or incites the destruction of an entire group.
words.e: The broadcast was laced with *genocidal rhetoric* aimed at the minority population.

words.d: Wrongly merging two distinct things into one.
words.e: You're *conflating* criticism of the policy with hatred of the country — they aren't the same.
words.a: يَخلِط بين أمرين مختلفين ويجعلهما واحدًا

words.d: Shockingly bad; outstandingly terrible.
words.e: The witness told *egregious* lies under oath and was later charged with perjury.

words.d: To brag openly and without shame.
words.e: He *brazenly boasted* about breaking the rules, as if daring anyone to stop him.

words.d: Confirmed by additional independent evidence.
words.e: Her testimony was *corroborated* by three separate witnesses.

words.d: Hard to believe; not convincing.
words.e: His excuse was so *implausible* that even his allies rolled their eyes.

words.d: Referred to something indirectly, without naming it.
words.e: She *alluded* to problems in the company without ever naming who was responsible.

words.d: To happen — or, in formal use, to become known.
words.e: No one knows exactly what *transpired* behind those closed doors.

words.d: Deliberately deceptive; two-faced.
words.e: His *duplicitous* nature meant you could never trust what he said behind closed doors.

words.d: Going in circles without ever reaching the point. From the nursery rhyme.
words.e: We've been going round the *mulberry bush* on this for an hour — let's decide.
words.a: يدور في حلقة مفرغة دون الوصول للُبّ الموضوع

words.d: Cruelly and without feeling; indifferent to others' suffering.
words.e: He *callously* ignored the injured man lying in the road.

words.d: Deeply desired — often something that belongs to someone else.
words.e: She *coveted* her neighbour's garden and spent years trying to outdo it.
words.a: مطموع فيه — يشتهيه بشدّة، خاصة ما يملكه غيره

words.d: Boldly rude and disrespectful, especially to a superior.
words.e: The servant gave an *insolent* reply and was dismissed on the spot.
words.a: وَقِح، سليط اللسان مع من هو أعلى منه

words.d: Humble; low in rank or importance.
words.e: He rose from *lowly* origins to become the most powerful man in the city.

words.d: Flattering the powerful excessively in order to gain something.
words.e: He surrounded himself with *sycophantic* friends who agreed with everything he said.

words.d: Dark, grave or gloomy in mood. (British spelling: sombre.)
words.e: The funeral was a *somber* affair, with few words spoken.

words.d: Persistent determination; refusing to give up.
words.e: Her *tenacity* kept her going through years of failure before she finally succeeded.

words.d: To relax idly; to do nothing productive.
words.e: He spent the whole summer *lazing* by the river instead of working the fields.

words.d: Taking pleasure in being merely average; being content with low standards.
words.e: The team was *reveling in mediocrity*, celebrating small wins while their rivals dominated.

words.d: Bullied into submission by relentless pressure.
words.e: She was *browbeaten* by her manager into accepting unpaid overtime.

words.d: To whine and complain persistently. British and Australian; rhymes with 'hinge'.
words.e: Stop *whingeing* about the weather and just bring an umbrella.

words.d: To feel quiet anger at an unwelcome burden placed on you.
words.e: She *resents the imposition* of having to host her in-laws every holiday.

words.d: Generosity and nobility of spirit, especially toward a defeated rival.
words.e: The queen showed *magnanimity* by pardoning the rebels rather than executing them.
words.a: شهامة وكرم نفس، خاصة تجاه الخصم

words.d: Attractively exciting; full of charm and polish.
words.e: The *glamorous* lifestyle of film stars hid years of grueling work.

words.d: Preparing land for crops — or patiently developing a skill or relationship over time.
words.e: She spent years *cultivating* relationships with influential people in the industry.
words.a: يزرع ويرعى؛ ومجازًا: يبني مهارة أو علاقة بصبر

words.d: Severe mental or physical suffering. Stronger than sadness — it implies torment.
words.e: She waited in *anguish* for news of the missing children.

words.d: The habit of expecting the worst outcome. Opposite of optimism.
words.e: Years of failed negotiations bred a deep *pessimism* about any lasting peace.

words.d: To keep going despite difficulty or repeated failure.
words.e: He *persevered* through three rejections before the paper was finally accepted.
words.n: Persevere is the action; tenacity (above) is the quality that makes you do it.

words.d: Impossible to satisfy — a hunger, curiosity or demand that never fills up.
words.e: The city had an *insatiable* appetite for water that the river simply could not meet.

words.d: Extremely thorough, careful and demanding.
words.e: The experiment required *rigorous* methodology — every variable had to be controlled.

words.d: Based on reason and logic rather than emotion.
words.e: She made a *rational* decision to sell the house, even though it broke her heart.
words.a: عقلاني، قائم على المنطق لا العاطفة

words.d: Belonging to something by its very nature; built in, not added.
words.e: Curiosity is an *intrinsic* part of being human.

words.d: To apply force, effort or influence.
words.e: She had to *exert* all her strength to push the door open against the wind.
words.a: يبذل جهدًا، يُمارِس قوة أو نفوذًا

words.d: Being completely forgotten; or total destruction and nothingness.
words.e: The empire crumbled into *oblivion*, and within a century no one remembered its name.

words.d: A feeling that something — usually bad — is about to happen.
words.e: She couldn't shake the *presentiment* that something terrible awaited them.

words.d: The past tense of 'seek': looked for, or tried to obtain.
words.e: He *sought* answers in old books that no one else had opened in decades.

words.d: In a way so strange or exact that it feels supernatural.
words.e: The prediction proved *uncannily* accurate — every detail came true.
words.a: بشكل غريب مُريب يكاد يكون خارقًا

words.d: Kept different parts of life or knowledge strictly separate.
words.e: He *compartmentalized* work and family so completely that his colleagues knew nothing about his children.
words.a: يفصل جوانب حياته فصلًا تامًّا في حجرات مستقلة

words.d: Based on guesswork or theory rather than firm evidence.
words.e: His claims about the company's future were highly *speculative*.
words.a: تخميني، قائم على الظنّ لا الدليل

words.d: The purest, most perfect example of a type — the one you'd point to if you had to explain the whole category.
words.e: That corner café is the *quintessential example* of what the neighbourhood used to be.

words.d: Existing as a permanent, inseparable part of something.
words.e: There is an *inherent* risk in any surgery, however routine it seems.
words.a: متأصّل، ملازم لا ينفصل عن الشيء
words.n: Nearly identical to 'intrinsic'. Inherent leans toward risks and problems that come with a thing; intrinsic leans toward value and nature.

words.d: Placed side by side so the contrast between two things becomes obvious.
words.e: The photographer *juxtaposed* the palace and the slum on facing pages.
words.a: موضوع جنبًا إلى جنب لإبراز التباين

words.d: Clear and easy to follow. Of a person: mentally clear, not confused.
words.e: Her explanation was so *lucid* that even the beginners followed it.
words.a: واضح جليّ سهل الفهم؛ وللشخص: صافي الذهن

words.d: Extremely careful about small details.
words.e: The forger was *meticulous*, matching even the age of the paper.

words.d: To make something bad less severe. It reduces harm; it does not remove it.
words.e: Planting trees will not stop the flooding, but it may *mitigate* the damage.
words.a: يُخفِّف من حدّة الضرر (دون أن يمنعه)

words.d: Just beginning to exist and not yet developed. Pronounced NAY-sent.
words.e: The *nascent* industry employed only a few hundred people at the time.

words.d: A subtle shade of meaning or difference that a rough summary would lose.
words.e: His argument ignored every *nuance* and treated the issue as purely black and white.
words.a: فارق دقيق في المعنى، ظِلال المعنى

words.d: A statement or situation that contradicts itself and yet may still be true.
words.e: It is a *paradox* that the more choices we have, the harder it becomes to choose.
words.a: مفارقة — قول يناقض نفسه وقد يكون صحيحًا

words.d: Able to be hammered into shape. Of a person: easily influenced.
words.e: Young recruits are *malleable*, which is exactly why the training begins so early.
words.a: طَيِّع قابل للتشكيل؛ وللشخص: سهل التأثّر

words.d: Strange in a way that frightens you — quietly wrong rather than openly threatening.
words.e: The abandoned streets had an *eerie* silence about them.
words.n: Spelled eerie, with two e's at the front. 'Erie' is a lake in North America.

words.d: A small gnawing mammal — rats, mice, squirrels.
words.e: The barn was overrun with *rodents* that chewed through the grain sacks.

words.d: A small, round, peppery root vegetable, usually red-skinned and white inside.
words.e: She pulled a handful of *radishes* from the garden and rinsed them for the salad.

words.d: A painful bubble of fluid on the skin, caused by friction or burning.
words.e: Her new boots gave her *blisters* on both heels.
words.a: بَثْرة ماء في الجلد من الاحتكاك أو الحرق

words.d: A limb or part extending from a main body — or anything treated as a minor attachment to something larger.
words.e: The small office felt like an *appendage of* headquarters: overlooked and underfunded.
words.a: طَرَف أو زائدة؛ ومجازًا: تابع ملحق بشيء أكبر

words.d: A repulsive bend or distortion — 'vile' supplies the disgust, 'curvature' the shape.
words.e: The inspector condemned the *vile curvature* of the cheaply built walls.

words.d: To seize and carry off by force; also, to fill someone with intense delight.
words.e: The audience was *ravished* by the beauty of the performance.
words.a: يَخطَف بالقوة؛ وأيضًا: يأخذ باللُّبّ من شدة الجمال
words.n: It also means to rape. Because of that, most writers now avoid it entirely — recognise it, don't use it.

words.d: Corrupted by excessive indulgence in drink and sensual pleasure.
words.e: The nobleman *debauched* himself upon wine and women until his fortune was gone.

words.d: Relating to sexually transmitted disease. From Venus, goddess of love.
words.e: The soldiers returned from the port city riddled with *venereal* disease.
words.n: Medically dated — today you'd say STI. Common in historical writing.

words.d: A food or substance believed to arouse sexual desire.
words.e: Oysters have long been considered an *aphrodisiac*, though the science is thin.

words.d: A person who helps someone else commit a crime.
words.e: The driver was arrested as an *accomplice* to the robbery.

words.d: To search through waste and ruins for something usable, especially food.
words.e: After the siege, the survivors were forced to *scavenge for food* in the rubble.
words.a: ينبش في المخلَّفات بحثًا عن طعام أو نافع

words.d: Gathering in large numbers or quantities.
words.e: Refugees were *amassing* at the border, seeking food and safety.

words.d: Evidence that you were somewhere else when a crime happened. Loosely, any convenient excuse.
words.e: His *alibi* collapsed when the restaurant's cameras showed he had left at nine.
words.a: دفع بالغيبة — إثبات وجوده في مكان آخر وقت الجريمة

words.d: A system of enforced racial segregation — specifically South Africa's state policy from 1948 to 1994. Pronounced a-PART-hate.
words.e: Under *apartheid*, where a person could live, work and travel was decided by race.

words.d: Imprisoned. The formal word used in law, journalism and policy writing.
words.e: He was *incarcerated* for eleven years before the conviction was finally overturned.

words.d: A person's health and wellbeing — and also the government payments that support people who cannot support themselves.
words.e: The charity was founded for the *welfare* of children orphaned by the war.
words.a: رفاه وسلامة؛ وأيضًا: إعانات الدولة للفقراء

words.d: Minor criminal behaviour, especially by young people. Also, failure to meet an obligation such as a payment.
words.e: Rising youth *delinquency* was blamed on the closure of the city's schools.
words.a: جُنوح — انحراف سلوكي خاصة عند الأحداث

words.d: Something persistently annoying. In law, an activity that unreasonably interferes with neighbours.
words.e: The barking became such a *nuisance* that the neighbours filed a formal complaint.
words.a: إزعاج مستمر، مصدر ضيق (وفي القانون: ضرر بالجيران)

words.d: An overwhelming presence of pests — insects, rats, weeds.
words.e: The building had a rat *infestation* that the landlord refused to address.
words.n: Applied to people it is dehumanising language and a recognised marker of hate speech. Note where you see it used that way.

words.d: Routine, unglamorous household tasks that must be repeated.
words.e: The children divided the *chores*: one swept the yard, the other fetched water.

words.d: Extreme and widespread scarcity of food across a whole region.
words.e: The *famine* killed more people than the war that had caused it.

words.d: Small and clearly inadequate in quantity. (British spelling: meagre.)
words.e: They survived on a *meager* ration of rice and lentils.

words.d: Extremely poor — lacking even the basic means to live.
words.e: The fire left forty families *destitute*, with nothing but the clothes they were wearing.
words.a: معدَم، فقير لا يملك قوت يومه

words.d: Abnormally thin and weak from starvation or long illness.
words.e: The rescued animals were *emaciated*, their ribs visible through their coats.
words.a: هزيل مُنهَك من الجوع أو المرض

words.d: Suffering from a lack of food or of the right nutrients.
words.e: One in five children in the camp was severely *malnourished*.
words.n: Malnourished is about diet; emaciated is about the visible body. Someone can be malnourished without looking it.

words.d: Sluggish and drained of energy.
words.e: Weeks of poor food left the workers *lethargic* and unable to concentrate.

words.d: The general population of a place, considered as a whole.
words.e: The announcement was met with anger from the *populace*.
words.n: Populace = the people. Populous = having many people. Different words.

words.d: Wealthy; comfortably well off.
words.e: She grew up in an *affluent family* that never worried about the cost of anything.

words.d: Originating naturally in a place. Of people: the original inhabitants of a land, predating settlers.
words.e: *Indigenous* communities had farmed the valley for centuries before the survey arrived.
words.n: Capitalised as 'Indigenous' when referring to peoples, in most modern style guides.

words.d: To calm someone down. Of a territory: to subdue it and end resistance.
words.e: The general claimed to have *pacified* the province, though the raids never truly stopped.
words.n: The military sense is a euphemism — 'pacified' can describe an occupation. Worth noticing who is using it.

words.d: Quiet, obedient and easy to control.
words.e: The regime preferred a *docile* press that printed whatever it was given.
